examples.solution_text:
Keep both terms and change the sign between them.
$3\sqrt{7}+2$

Use the difference of two squares.
$\begin{aligned}&\mathrel{\phantom{=}}(3\sqrt{5}+2)(3\sqrt{5}-2)\\&=(3\sqrt{5})^2-2^2\\&=9\times5-4\\&=41\end{aligned}$

examples.question_text: Rationalise the denominator of $\dfrac{5}{2-\sqrt{7}}$, giving your answer in simplest form.
examples.solution_text:
Multiply the numerator and denominator by the conjugate, $2+\sqrt{7}$.
$\begin{aligned}&\mathrel{\phantom{=}}\dfrac{5}{2-\sqrt{7}}\\&=\dfrac{5}{2-\sqrt{7}}\times\dfrac{2+\sqrt{7}}{2+\sqrt{7}}\\&=\dfrac{10+5\sqrt{7}}{2^2-(\sqrt{7})^2}\\&=\dfrac{10+5\sqrt{7}}{-3}\\&=-\dfrac{10+5\sqrt{7}}{3}\end{aligned}$

examples.question_text: Rationalise the denominator of $\dfrac{4}{\sqrt{11}+\sqrt{7}}$, giving your answer in simplest form.
Rationalise the denominator of $\dfrac{\sqrt{6}}{\sqrt{10}-\sqrt{2}}$, giving your answer in simplest form.
examples.solution_text:
Multiply by the conjugate, $\sqrt{10}+\sqrt{2}$, then simplify the numerator's surds.
$\begin{aligned}&\mathrel{\phantom{=}}\dfrac{\sqrt{6}}{\sqrt{10}-\sqrt{2}}\\&=\dfrac{\sqrt{6}}{\sqrt{10}-\sqrt{2}}\times\dfrac{\sqrt{10}+\sqrt{2}}{\sqrt{10}+\sqrt{2}}\\&=\dfrac{\sqrt{60}+\sqrt{12}}{10-2}\\&=\dfrac{2\sqrt{15}+2\sqrt{3}}{8}\\&=\dfrac{\sqrt{15}+\sqrt{3}}{4}\end{aligned}$

The conjugate is $4+\sqrt{3}$, so the numerator becomes a perfect square.
$\begin{aligned}&\mathrel{\phantom{=}}\dfrac{4+\sqrt{3}}{4-\sqrt{3}}\\&=\dfrac{4+\sqrt{3}}{4-\sqrt{3}}\times\dfrac{4+\sqrt{3}}{4+\sqrt{3}}\\&=\dfrac{(4+\sqrt{3})^2}{4^2-(\sqrt{3})^2}\\&=\dfrac{16+8\sqrt{3}+3}{16-3}\\&=\dfrac{19+8\sqrt{3}}{13}\end{aligned}$

Multiply by the conjugate, $3\sqrt{2}+\sqrt{5}$. Square the coefficient as well as the surd in the denominator.
$\begin{aligned}&\mathrel{\phantom{=}}\dfrac{3}{3\sqrt{2}-\sqrt{5}}\\&=\dfrac{3}{3\sqrt{2}-\sqrt{5}}\times\dfrac{3\sqrt{2}+\sqrt{5}}{3\sqrt{2}+\sqrt{5}}\\&=\dfrac{9\sqrt{2}+3\sqrt{5}}{(3\sqrt{2})^2-(\sqrt{5})^2}\\&=\dfrac{9\sqrt{2}+3\sqrt{5}}{18-5}\\&=\dfrac{9\sqrt{2}+3\sqrt{5}}{13}\end{aligned}$

examples.question_text: Simplify $\dfrac{1}{4+\sqrt{6}}+\dfrac{1}{4-\sqrt{6}}$ and show that the result is rational.
examples.solution_text:
Use the product of the conjugate denominators as the lowest common denominator.
$\begin{aligned}&\mathrel{\phantom{=}}\dfrac{1}{4+\sqrt{6}}+\dfrac{1}{4-\sqrt{6}}\\&=\dfrac{4-\sqrt{6}+4+\sqrt{6}}{(4+\sqrt{6})(4-\sqrt{6})}\\&=\dfrac{8}{16-6}\\&=\dfrac{4}{5}\end{aligned}$
The result is rational because it is a ratio of integers.

examples.question_text: $\dfrac{\sqrt{13}+1}{\sqrt{13}-1}$ can be written as $\dfrac{a+b\sqrt{13}}{6}$, where $a$ and $b$ are integers. Find $a$ and $b$.
examples.solution_text:
Rationalise the denominator, then compare the numerator with the required form.
$\begin{aligned}&\mathrel{\phantom{=}}\dfrac{\sqrt{13}+1}{\sqrt{13}-1}\\&=\dfrac{\sqrt{13}+1}{\sqrt{13}-1}\times\dfrac{\sqrt{13}+1}{\sqrt{13}+1}\\&=\dfrac{13+2\sqrt{13}+1}{13-1}\\&=\dfrac{14+2\sqrt{13}}{12}\\&=\dfrac{7+\sqrt{13}}{6}\end{aligned}$
$a=7$ and $b=1$.

Each has separate editable question and solution fields; solution prose and mathematics inherit renderer blue. Continuation calculations have phantom equals gutters inside single-dollar aligned spans. These algebraic tasks need no diagrams. examples.derivation: Reversing the sign between the unchanged terms gives 3√7+2.
Multiplication by (2+√7)/(2+√7) gives numerator 10+5√7 and denominator 4−7=−3, hence −(10+5√7)/3.
The numerator becomes (4+√3)²=19+8√3; the denominator is 16−3=13. The result is (19+8√3)/13.
Multiplying by the conjugate gives numerator 9√2+3√5 and denominator (3√2)²−(√5)²=18−5=13.
Combining over the conjugate product gives ((4−√6)+(4+√6))/(16−6)=8/10=4/5, a ratio of integers.
Rationalisation gives (√13+1)²/(13−1)=(14+2√13)/12=(7+√13)/6. Comparing the specified numerator gives a=7 and b=1.
